newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Red Cross killings show fragile Chechnya peace.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross killings show fragile Chechnya peace.

text.p: The murder of six Western medical aid workers and the seizure of a group of Russian policemen by a radical rebel commander have highlighted the fragility of the peace process in breakaway Chechnya.

They will certainly not be the last tragedies in the devastated land teeming with arms, bandits and with the unfinished vendettas of men whose families and friends have been killed in 21 months of fighting and bombardment.
But neither Moscow nor the separatists who now run Chechnya are likely to allow the incidents to lead to the resumption of the all-out war, in which tens of thousands were killed.
President Boris Yeltsin, who sent thousands of troops into Chechnya in December 1994 to crush its three-year independence drive, cannot afford to let any more Russian soldiers die.

The army, unpaid and humiliated in 21 months of fighting, is clearly unwilling to return. The budget will not stand the costs of another war, which would also trigger protests from the West and liberals at home.
And Yeltsin, who has said the decision to use force in Chechnya may have been his worst political mistake, does not want to be seen reversing course again.
The rebels, on the other hand, need peace to ensure Moscow delivers on promises of economic aid to help them exploit their oil riches and restart the Chechen oil processing industry.
Rebel leaders due to compete in a presidential election scheduled for January 27 want the poll to become a symbol of their ability to conduct affairs in a "civilised" way.

They are also keen to have Russian troops withdrawn from the region, hoping that the pullout and a legitimate election will set them firmly on the road to their cherished goal of independence from Moscow.

Yeltsin, who still insists that Chechnya must remain part of the Russian Federation, decided to opt for peace after a dismal military campaign in which the Russian forces were unable to score a decisive victory.
The decision, accompanied by the sacking of Kremlin hawks largely blamed for the use of force, helped him to win a second presidential term.
A top presidential official, speaking on condition of anonymity, acknowleged last week that the Kremlin was paying a high price for its failure in the separatist region.
"We know that the confidence level after Chechnya is down to zero, we simply cannot take any resolute political steps after it," the official said.

The Kremlin made clear its intention to keep the peace process on track immediately after six employees of the International Committee of the Red Cross, five of them women, were killed in their beds on Tuesday.

"One has to count on the fact that, despite tragic excesses like these, ...the peace process will nevertheless be maintained and will develop," Yeltsin's press secretary, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, told a news conference.
Ministers of the Chechen government denounced the killing of the Red Cross workers as a provocation aimed at disrupting the peace process and preparation for elections.

Leaders such as Aslan Maskhadov, acting prime minister and former chief of staff of the Chechen resistance, face a delicate task in trying to rein in militant fighters like Salman Raduyev, who captured a group of Russian policemen on Saturday.
Russian news agencies say Maskhadov ordered Raduyev to free the captives and sent a top level Chechen government delegation to negotiate their release.

But he can hardly use force against the man with whom he fought just a few months ago and who is seen by a radical part of the Chechen youth as a hero after his hostage-taking raid into Russia at the start of this year.
